citations.quote: There are three subtypes of checkpoints that vary in their aggressiveness: PASSIVE, FULL, and RESTART.

citations.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.claim_text: Calling sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() always produces a FULL or RESTART checkpoint.
claims.reasoning: The passages only state the converse: FULL and RESTART checkpoints can only be initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2(). Nothing states that every call to sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() yields a FULL or RESTART checkpoint; other modes (e.g., the TRUNCATE option mentioned for manual checkpoints) are not ruled out.

claims.claim_text: A PASSIVE checkpoint is guaranteed to run to completion as long as no other connection is writing.
claims.reasoning: The passages say a PASSIVE checkpoint might not run to completion if there are concurrent readers or writers, and that an open read transaction alone (with no writer) can prevent a checkpoint from completing or resetting the WAL. Absence of writers is therefore not sufficient to guarantee completion.

citations.quote: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can without interfering with other database connections, and which might not run to completion if there are concurrent readers or writers.
Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
If another connection has a read transaction open, then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file because doing so might delete content out from under the reader.

claims.claim_text: A checkpoint can only reset the WAL when no other connection is using it.
claims.reasoning: Passage 7 states that running to completion and resetting the WAL requires that no other database connections are using the WAL file.

citations.quote: A checkpoint is only able to run to completion, and reset the WAL file, if there are no other database connections using the WAL file.

claims.claim_text: A checkpoint will always reset the WAL whenever the WAL is unused.
claims.reasoning: The passage states only a necessary condition (no other connections using the WAL) for a checkpoint to be able to reset the WAL. It never claims that an unused WAL is sufficient to guarantee that a checkpoint will reset it; the claim improperly converts a necessary condition into a sufficient one.

claims.claim_text: The automatic checkpoint is implemented on top of sqlite3_wal_hook().
claims.reasoning: Passage 4 states the automatic checkpoint mechanism is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook().

citations.quote: (The automatic checkpoint mechanism is implemented as a simple wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook().)

claims.claim_text: The automatic checkpoint runs in the same thread as the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.
claims.reasoning: Passage 3 states that by default the automatic checkpoint is run by the same thread that performs the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

citations.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.claim_text: Long-running readers never delay the automatic checkpoint.
claims.reasoning: The passages explicitly state that long-running read transactions can prevent a checkpointer from making progress, that an open read transaction prevents the checkpoint from resetting the WAL, and that with always-active readers no checkpoints can complete at all.

citations.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
If another connection has a read transaction open, then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file because doing so might delete content out from under the reader.

However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.claim_text: In WAL mode, SQLite normally keeps the WAL file in check automatically, so in the vast majority of cases applications need not worry about it.
claims.reasoning: The passages state that SQLite automatically takes care of the WAL file in the vast majority of cases and that the checkpoint/rewind mechanism prevents unbounded WAL growth.

citations.quote: So in the vast majority of cases, applications need not worry about the WAL file at all. SQLite will automatically take care of it.
This mechanism prevents a WAL file from growing without bound.

claims.claim_text: In its default configuration, SQLite automatically checkpoints the WAL file at the end of any transaction once it exceeds 1000 pages.
claims.reasoning: Directly stated in passage 3.

citations.quote: In its default configuration, SQLite will checkpoint the WAL file at the conclusion of any transaction when the WAL file is more than 1000 pages long.

claims.claim_text: Checkpointing transfers the entire WAL into the database and rewinds the WAL back to the beginning so that new transactions start at the beginning of the WAL.
claims.reasoning: Passage 1 describes the WAL being transferred into the database and the writer rewinding the WAL to the beginning and starting new transactions there.

citations.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning and start putting new transactions at the beginning of the WAL.

claims.claim_text: Several situations can defeat the automatic mechanism and cause the WAL file to grow without bound, causing excess disk space usage and slow query speeds.
claims.reasoning: Passage 2 states it is possible to get SQLite into a state where the WAL grows without bound and that the following bullets enumerate ways this can happen.

claims.claim_text: Compile-time and run-time options exist that can disable or defer the automatic checkpoint, and if an application disables the automatic checkpoint, nothing prevents the WAL file from growing excessively.
claims.reasoning: Directly stated in passage 3.

citations.quote: However, compile-time and run-time options exist that can disable or defer this automatic checkpoint. If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively.

claims.claim_text: Checkpoint starvation is a cause of unbounded WAL growth: a checkpoint can only run to completion and reset the WAL file if there are no other database connections using the WAL file.
claims.reasoning: Passage 4 names and defines checkpoint starvation, stating the condition under which a checkpoint can run to completion and reset the WAL.

citations.quote: Checkpoint starvation. A checkpoint is only able to run to completion, and reset the WAL file, if there are no other database connections using the WAL file.

claims.claim_text: A database with many concurrent overlapping readers and at least one always-active reader will never let a checkpoint finish, and the WAL file will grow without bound.
claims.reasoning: Directly stated in passage 5.

citations.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.claim_text: The WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction, so a large change to a large database can produce a very large WAL file until the transaction completes, at which point it will be checkpointed.
claims.reasoning: Directly stated in passage 7.

citations.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file. The WAL file will be checkpointed once the write transaction completes (assuming there are no other readers blocking it) but in the meantime, the file can grow very big.

claims.claim_text: On SQLite versions before 3.11.0, a transaction that grows larger than the page cache could write the same page into the WAL multiple times.
claims.reasoning: Passage 8 states that with older versions of SQLite (i.e., before 3.11.0), the same page might be written into the WAL multiple times if the transaction grows larger than the page cache.

citations.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself.

claims.claim_text: To keep the WAL under control, applications should leave automatic checkpointing enabled.
claims.reasoning: Passage 3 describes the consequence of disabling the automatic checkpoint, but no passage explicitly states the recommendation that applications should leave automatic checkpointing enabled.

claims.reasoning: Passage 0 notes that a long-running read transaction can block checkpoint progress and that read transactions presumably end eventually, but no passage explicitly advises keeping read transactions short.

citations.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.claim_text: For applications with many concurrent readers, running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option guarantees the checkpoint runs to completion before returning.

citations.quote: In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint runs to completion before returning.
